sentences.text: The only known species within the extinct genus Yaverlandia is Yaverlandia bitholus, which serves as the type species for the genus.
This animal measured approximately 1 meter in length and 30 centimeters in height, leaving behind only a thick skull with two marked bumps on the dome.
The skull is characterized by two small domes, a pitted dorsal surface, and specific features of the frontal and supratemporal fenestra.
The environment where Yaverlandia lived experienced frequent wildfires that stifled dense plant growth.
Most vertebrate fossils from the Wessex Formation, including Yaverlandia, come from plant debris beds caused by flooding.
The holotype was discovered in 1923 by F. M. G. Abell on the Isle of Wight, and the first specimen of Yaverlandia was described in 1930 by D. M. S. Watson.
Peter Galton recognized Yaverlandia as a distinct genus in 1971 after re-examining the remains, creating a cast of the specimen to aid his examination and naming the fossil as a pachycephalosaurid.
A second specimen of Yaverlandia was discovered in 2012 by a student during a school fossil hunt, and Naish and Steven C. Sweetman described the second specimen in 2026.
Additional remains were reported in 2012, but they have not yet been described.
Peter Galton believed Yaverlandia was the oldest member of the family Pachycephalosauridae.
Yaverlandia is classified within the superorder Dinosauria, belongs to the parent group Theropoda, and is classified in the class Reptilia.
Yaverlandia is tentatively classified within the unranked family Maniraptora, a classification supported by works ranging from 2000 to 2008 by Sullivan, Sereno, and Naish.
Yaverlandia is an extinct genus found in Lower Cretaceous strata of the Wessex Formation on the Isle of Wight, England, though fossils are now identified from the underlying Vectis Formation.
The fossils date to the Hauterivian and Barremian ages of the Wealden Group, with a time range from 132.6 to 121.4 million years ago.
Yaverlandia lived approximately 125 million years ago during the Barremian stage of the early Cretaceous in what is now Europe.

Darren Naish suggested in 2008 that Yaverlandia may be related to maniraptoran theropods, later suggesting it was a maniraptoran theropod rather than a pachycephalosaurid, and in 2011 proposing it was a troodontid, though his redescription has not yet been published.

Recent research suggests Yaverlandia's identity is enigmatic, with features comparable to both dinosaurs and non-dinosaurian reptiles like crocodyliforms, and researchers noted that no anatomical features definitively support placing Yaverlandia in any specific clade, including maniraptoran theropods or pachycephalosaurs, leading Naish and Sweetman to conclude that the phylogenetic affinities of Yaverlandia remain unclear.
